analysis.one_liner: Imposes inspections, tenant rights, health screening, and financial disclosure on privatized military housing, and bars officials from owning stakes in it.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and never advanced; it died at the end of the 116th Congress without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Most families on military bases live in housing owned and run by private companies paid with service members' housing allowances. After reports of mold, lead, rats, and slow repairs, this bill would have required independent inspectors, no-notice inspections by state and local officials, public disclosure of what the companies earn, and a process letting service members stop paying rent when a unit is unlivable. It would also have banned members of Congress on defense committees, senior defense officials, and senior officers from owning stakes in the private housing companies, and given veterans and their families VA care for illnesses linked to bad housing. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Military families living in privatized on-base housing, who would gain enforceable inspections, written tenant rights, the ability to stop their housing allowance when a unit is uninhabitable, relocation and medical costs paid by negligent landlords, a public complaint database, and — for veterans and their families — VA healthcare and disability presumptions for illnesses linked to bad housing.

how_it_helps.text: Service members could file a claim to stop their housing allowance from going to a landlord whose unit was uninhabitable or poorly maintained, with rent reduced 10% for every five days a problem went unfixed and the reduction returned to the tenant.

Independent certified inspectors would conduct no-notice inspections, and state and local inspectors could inspect units on military installations—closing a gap that had left military housing largely outside local code enforcement.

Military treatment facilities would screen families for illnesses linked to unsafe housing, landlords would pay medical bills tied to substandard conditions, and veterans with housing-linked illnesses would get a presumption of service connection for disability benefits, with their family members eligible for VA care.

Landlords would be barred from marking maintenance complete without the tenant's written approval, and all state and local tenant protections—including habitability standards and eviction defenses—would apply inside military housing.

Contract finances—management fees, incentive fees, and residual cash distributions—would be published in the Federal Register and landlords would file 10-K-equivalent financial statements posted publicly, so families and Congress could see where the housing allowance money was going.

analysis.who_pays: Private military housing companies, through rent reductions, relocation costs, medical bills, and public disclosure of their fees and finances; senior defense officials and defense-committee members would have faced a new ownership ban.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have shifted significant costs onto private housing companies—rent reductions of 10% per five days of unresolved disrepair, relocation costs, medical bills, and detailed public disclosure of management and incentive fees—which companies could argue would raise the cost or risk of building and maintaining military housing.

Allowing state and local inspectors to conduct no-notice inspections on military installations, and letting service members stop housing payments while disputes were investigated, would have added administrative complexity to the housing offices and created potential for disputed habitability findings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to service members and their families are concrete: safer housing, faster fixes, an easy way to stop paying rent on a moldy or unsafe unit, and healthcare if the housing made them sick. The costs fall on private housing companies, which would bear inspection outcomes, rent reductions, relocation bills, medical bills, and public disclosure of their profits. The strongest good-faith objections: the private-housing model itself exists because Congress eliminated direct military construction in the 1990s, so squeezing companies too hard could drive them out and leave housing unprovided; and no-notice state and local inspections on bases raised questions about consistency with military security practices. The bill's design was reasonable—it kept the housing companies in place and attached accountability to the money already flowing to them—but it received no committee consideration, so no amended version was ever weighed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, then to subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it, so it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 29, 2019 and referred to three committees—Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, and Judiciary—and then to subcommittees on Readiness, Disability Assistance and Memorial Affairs, and Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security.
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind followed; the last recorded action was the subcommittee referral on May 20, 2019.
With the 116th Congress ending January 3, 2021, the bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private companies that manage military housing under DoD contracts, which face no new inspections, tenant remedies, fee disclosures, or liability as a result. Officials with financial interests in military housing also keep freedoms the bill would have removed.

for.name: 21 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor signed on.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for consideration and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Private military housing companies
against.role: Privatized housing operators under DoD contracts
against.what_they_did: The bill's transparency, inspection, and tenant-remedy provisions directly targeted companies managing most on-base housing; their opposition to similar measures during this period was widely reported, though no lobby record appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 initial supporters, including 21 of the eventual 21 cosponsors, were Democrats; no Republican ever signed on, but the bill also never got far enough for a roll-call vote to show where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Private military housing companies (public-private partnership landlords)
industries.note: The bill would have subjected them to independent inspections, standardized leases, rent reductions for failed maintenance, mandatory relocation and medical payments, a public complaint database, and public disclosure of their contract fees and financial statements. It would have regulated them rather than displaced them, but sharply cut into their autonomy and profits from housing allowances.

industries.industry: Officeholders and defense officials with financial stakes in military housing
industries.note: Members of Congress on the armed services committees, senior Pentagon civilians, and senior officers (O-6 and above) would have been barred from owning interests in entities that own or manage military housing, with civil penalties for violations.

Not an industry, but the intended beneficiary: safer housing, tenant remedies, medical screening and coverage for housing-linked illnesses, and disability presumptions for veterans who lived in unsafe units.
